paragraphs: Sequential decision problems can require more than keeping average costs low: the variability of those costs can also matter. This paper studies policies in Markov decision processes using a mean-CVaR objective. The objective combines the usual concern with expected cost and a risk measure intended to address shortcomings of variance-based measures.

The authors first derive a formula for the gradient of this objective. That formula provides a direction for changing a policy's parameters to improve its treatment of cost and risk. They then construct policy-gradient and actor-critic algorithms, each using its own method to estimate the gradient and update the policy.

The theoretical result establishes convergence to locally risk-sensitive optimal policies. The word locally matters: the claim concerns optimality around the resulting policy, rather than identifying the best policy everywhere. An optimal-stopping example demonstrates the algorithms' usefulness. Together, the gradient formula and algorithms provide a way to incorporate the stated risk objective directly into policy learning.
neurips-2014-algorithms-for-cvar-optimiz.tldr: The paper develops policy-gradient and actor-critic algorithms for mean-CVaR objectives and proves convergence to locally risk-sensitive optimal policies.

paragraphs: Bandit convex optimization provides a framework for making decisions under uncertainty. A central question is how much regret an algorithm must incur as it learns to make those decisions. The paper focuses on nonlinear losses, where the best attainable regret was less well understood than in the special case of linear costs.

The authors develop an efficient algorithm with a near-optimal regret guarantee for losses that are both strongly convex and smooth. Those two requirements define the setting of the result. The contribution therefore advances understanding of a structured nonlinear case, while leaving the broader question for nonlinear bandit convex optimization open.

The distinguishing design choice is an exploration scheme that shrinks over time. Earlier approaches discussed in the abstract use exploration schemes that remain unchanged over time. Here, the exploration schedule becomes part of the route to the regret guarantee. The stated finding connects this changing exploration strategy with efficient, near-optimal performance under the specified assumptions on the loss functions.
neurips-2014-bandit-convex-optimization-.tldr: A shrinking exploration scheme gives efficient, near-optimal regret guarantees for bandit convex optimization with strongly convex, smooth losses.

paragraphs: The paper studies how fixing selected variables can improve approximate inference in graphical models. Its starting point is a known result: for attractive binary pairwise models, the Bethe approximation to the partition function lies below the true value. The authors give a new proof built directly around fixing, or clamping, variables.

Clamping one variable to each possible value produces a collection of smaller sub-models. For an attractive model, the authors show that adding their Bethe partition functions can only increase the approximation. Because it remains a lower approximation, that increase improves it. Repeating this process until the remaining models contain no cycles reaches a setting where the Bethe approximation is exact.

This argument supplies both a proof technique and a practical strategy. The authors demonstrate that carefully choosing just a few variables to clamp can sharply reduce approximation error. They also derive a related topology-dependent lower bound for a broad class of approximate partition functions in general pairwise models with multiple labels. The monotonic improvement claim specifically concerns the attractive-model setting.
neurips-2014-clamping-variables-and-appr.tldr: Clamping variables improves Bethe partition-function approximations for attractive models and can substantially reduce practical approximation error.

paragraphs: Weighted expert voting combines judgments while allowing different experts to carry different influence. This paper examines the statistical reliability of the optimal Nitzan-Paroush weighted-majority rule and related voting rules. It studies both asymptotic consistency and finite-setting guarantees, connecting the behavior of voting procedures with explicit estimates of their errors.

A key distinction is whether expert competence is already known. When competence levels are available, the authors give sharp error estimates for the optimal voting rule. When those levels are unknown, they must first be estimated from observations. The paper analyzes this additional estimation problem through both frequentist and Bayesian approaches.

That separation matters because choosing voting weights with known competence and learning those weights from data are different statistical tasks. The paper provides nearly optimal bounds and uses experiments to illustrate its theoretical findings. It also introduces proof techniques that the authors suggest may have wider interest. The contribution is a statistical account of when weighted voting is reliable, including the uncertainty introduced by estimating expert competence.
neurips-2014-consistency-of-weighted-maj.tldr: The paper derives nearly optimal reliability bounds for weighted expert voting with either known or empirically estimated competence levels.

paragraphs: This paper asks when an existing convex clustering procedure can correctly recover cluster membership. The procedure uses sum-of-norms regularization, abbreviated SON. The contribution is a theoretical analysis of its behavior, aimed at explaining why the method works in a concrete setting rather than introducing another clustering algorithm.

The analyzed setting contains samples drawn from two cubes, with each cube representing a separate cluster. The authors prove that SON can identify membership when the distance between the cubes exceeds a specified threshold. That threshold depends linearly on the cube size and on the ratio between the numbers of samples in the two clusters.

The result makes the recovery guarantee depend explicitly on cluster geometry and relative sample counts. It is a sufficient separation condition for this two-cube setting; it does not state that recovery is impossible below the threshold. By tying a convex optimization procedure to a provable membership result, the analysis offers a concrete basis for understanding its behavior and potentially developing further convex approaches to clustering.
neurips-2014-convex-optimization-procedu.tldr: SON clustering provably recovers two cube-shaped clusters when their separation exceeds a threshold determined by cube size and relative sample counts.

paragraphs: Variational Gaussian inference approximates Bayesian inference by optimizing a lower bound on marginal likelihood. Its computational burden can grow quickly: with L latent dimensions, the usual formulation involves O(L²) variational parameters. Existing ways to reduce this number can sacrifice accuracy or disrupt concavity, making optimization slower.

The proposed method decouples the optimization through a Lagrangian formulation requiring O(N) parameters, where N is the number of examples. The authors establish a unique reparameterization that recovers maxima of the original lower bound even when that bound is nonconcave. The parameter count therefore depends on the number of examples rather than quadratically on latent dimensionality.

Optimization proceeds through a sequence of convex problems that can be parallelized across examples and support efficient gradient computation. The method avoids directly computing the covariance, using its linear projections instead. For concave bounds, its theoretical convergence rate matches existing methods; for nonconcave bounds, it remains convergent at a rate described as reasonable. These results connect reduced representation costs with convergence analysis across both settings.
neurips-2014-decoupled-variational-gauss.tldr: Decoupled variational inference reduces Gaussian variational parameters to O(N) and optimizes through parallelizable convex subproblems without directly computing covariance.

paragraphs: Image deconvolution becomes difficult when actual image degradation differs from an ideal linear blur model. Camera noise, saturation, and compression can all create such differences. This paper develops a convolutional neural network that learns characteristics of the degradation, addressing the challenge of explicitly modeling these effects within a generative approach.

The architecture is central to the proposal. The authors report that directly applying existing deep networks does not produce reasonable results. They instead connect traditional optimization-based methods to a neural network design and introduce a separable structure intended to support deconvolution that is robust to artifacts. The resulting network has two submodules, both trained with supervision and appropriate initialization.

The reported application is non-blind image deconvolution, and the authors describe performance as decent compared with earlier generative-model methods. The stated result supports the usefulness of a purpose-built architecture for this task without claiming universal superiority. Its broader methodological point is that optimization-based structure can guide a learned image-restoration system when a simple degradation model is inadequate.
neurips-2014-deep-convolutional-neural-n.tldr: A supervised convolutional network with an optimization-inspired separable structure addresses non-blind image deconvolution under imperfect blur models.

paragraphs: Extracting an object from an image involves locating it and deciding which pixels belong to it. This paper treats those activities as linked learning tasks. It introduces two convolutional networks that work together, aiming to locate salient objects quickly and then segment them accurately without handcrafted features or sliding-window approaches.

The first network predicts object positions and scales directly from the image. Latent variables connect its predictions to the second network by adjusting the localizations used to produce pixelwise object masks. This connection makes localization part of a joint optimization problem, so the two networks are trained as a collaborative system.

Training follows an EM-type alternating procedure. One step estimates the latent variables using MCMC-based sampling informed by both networks. The next holds those variables fixed and updates both networks through backpropagation. Experiments report substantial gains in accuracy and efficiency over competing approaches, including a speedup of 1,000 times in the reported comparisons. These findings support joint learning as a useful way to coordinate localization and segmentation.
neurips-2014-deep-joint-task-learning-fo.tldr: Two jointly trained convolutional networks connect object localization and segmentation through latent variables, with substantial reported accuracy and speed gains.

paragraphs: Distributed graph computation depends heavily on how a graph is divided across computing resources. A partition must keep workloads balanced while controlling communication between resources. The paper focuses on power-law graphs, whose highly uneven degree distributions make it difficult to achieve both goals with existing partitioning methods.

The authors propose degree-based hashing, or DBH, as a vertex-cut partitioning method. Its central design choice is to use the skewed degree distribution when constructing the partition. The same structural feature that makes these graphs challenging thus becomes information the partitioning method can exploit to organize distributed work.

The theoretical analysis shows that DBH can achieve lower communication costs than existing methods while also guaranteeing good workload balance. Experiments on several large power-law graphs provide additional evidence that it can outperform the state of the art. The importance of the result lies in addressing both costs together: reducing communication is useful alongside a partition that keeps work adequately distributed. The stated claims concern the power-law graph setting investigated in the paper.
neurips-2014-distributed-power-law-graph.tldr: Degree-based hashing uses power-law degree distributions to partition graphs with provable workload balance and potentially lower communication costs.

paragraphs: Low-rank tensor estimation is useful in many applications, but methods based on Schatten 1-norm minimization can become prohibitively slow as problems grow. This paper addresses that computational obstacle with a method that performs tensor decomposition and completion together. Its main idea is to move the expensive regularization calculation to a smaller representation.

The authors establish an equivalence relating the Schatten 1-norm of a low-rank tensor to that of its core tensor. They then replace the full-tensor norm with the core-tensor norm in the optimization. This turns the relevant computation into a substantially smaller matrix norm-minimization problem, reducing the computational complexity of the proposed formulation.

To solve it, the paper develops an efficient algorithm with a rank-increasing scheme and a convergence guarantee. Extensive experiments report that the method is usually more accurate than the compared state-of-the-art methods and faster by orders of magnitude. The accuracy claim is explicitly qualified by 'usually.' The central contribution is the mathematical reduction that makes a smaller core carry the costly computation needed for decomposition and completion.
neurips-2014-generalized-higher-order-or.tldr: Replacing full-tensor norm minimization with an equivalent core-tensor formulation enables scalable decomposition and completion with strong reported speed gains.

paragraphs: This paper separates two questions about learning an undirected graphical model: whether its parameters are determined by available information, and whether they can be computed efficiently. In a minimal exponential family, mean parameters uniquely determine canonical parameters. That uniqueness makes recovery well-defined, but it does not by itself provide an efficient algorithm.

The main theorem establishes a general computational obstacle. Unless RP equals NP, no algorithm can recover canonical parameters from mean parameters for generic pairwise binary graphical models in time polynomial in the number of variables. This is a general hardness result, rather than a claim that every particular model is difficult.

The proof reduces a known hard problem—approximating the hard-core model's partition function—to approximate parameter learning. An efficient solution to the latter would therefore solve the former. The reduction also establishes a repulsive property of the marginal polytope's boundary, supporting an optimization procedure that does not need knowledge of the polytope's structure. The result shows why statistical identifiability alone cannot guarantee computational feasibility.
neurips-2014-hardness-of-parameter-estim.tldr: Recovering graphical-model parameters from their means is generally computationally intractable unless RP equals NP, even when the parameters are uniquely determined.

paragraphs: Learning a shared representation across modalities does not automatically explain how well a model can infer a missing modality from the others. This paper makes that ability an explicit learning goal. It proposes a multimodal framework trained by minimizing variation of information, replacing maximum likelihood as the chosen training objective.

The authors provide theoretical insight into why this objective is sufficient to estimate the joint distribution generating the multimodal data. They apply the framework to restricted Boltzmann machines and develop learning methods using contrastive divergence and multi-prediction training. They also extend the approach to deep networks with recurrent encoding so that the entire network can be fine-tuned.

Experiments report state-of-the-art visual recognition performance on MIR-Flickr and PASCAL VOC 2007, both with and without text features. These results connect the proposed objective to recognition performance under different modality availability. The methodological contribution is a learning criterion aimed directly at relationships between modalities, supported by theory about joint-distribution estimation and implementations for both restricted Boltzmann machines and deeper networks.
neurips-2014-improved-multimodal-deep-le.tldr: Training multimodal models with variation of information targets missing-modality inference and yields strong reported visual recognition results.

paragraphs: The Convex Polytope Machine addresses large-scale binary classification with a nonlinear separator. It learns a large-margin convex polytope that surrounds one class. Its multiple sides provide the component boundaries of the classifier, allowing the decision rule to use a geometric enclosure rather than relying on a single separating boundary.

The authors develop a stochastic-gradient training algorithm suitable for massive datasets. They supplement it with a heuristic intended to avoid poor local minima. This combination addresses the practical optimization challenge of fitting the polytope, while the heuristic remains a practical device rather than a stated guarantee of finding a global optimum.

Experiments cover handwritten-digit recognition, text topics, and web security. The reported models train faster than comparable approaches and kernel SVMs, sometimes by several orders of magnitude, while attaining comparable or better classification performance. The results also suggest that controlling the number of polytope sides is unnecessary for avoiding overfitting in the evaluated settings. That last observation is empirical, rather than a universal guarantee about model size.
neurips-2014-large-margin-convex-polytop.tldr: The Convex Polytope Machine learns a nonlinear enclosure for one class, with substantially faster training and competitive accuracy in reported experiments.

paragraphs: Canonical correlation analysis is a widely used statistical tool with established theory and favorable results across many machine-learning problems. Its practical difficulty at large scale is computation: standard approaches require QR or singular-value decompositions of very large matrices. Those operations can make an otherwise useful analysis slow on huge datasets.

The paper introduces L-CCA, an iterative algorithm designed to compute CCA quickly on huge sparse datasets. The title identifies iterative least squares as the approach. The contribution centers on making the computation practical in this setting, where the size and sparsity of the data are central considerations.

The authors establish both asymptotic convergence and finite-time accuracy results. These address complementary questions: how the algorithm behaves as iteration continues, and how accurate its result is after a finite amount of computation. Experiments on two real datasets also report better performance than other fast CCA approximation schemes. Together, the theory and experiments support L-CCA as a scalable computational approach, with empirical comparisons limited to the two reported datasets.
neurips-2014-large-scale-canonical-corre.tldr: L-CCA computes canonical correlation analysis iteratively on huge sparse datasets, with convergence theory, finite-time accuracy results, and favorable empirical comparisons.

paragraphs: Object detection is difficult to scale because precise bounding-box annotations are expensive to collect. Image-level category labels are much easier to obtain, but a classifier trained on those labels does not directly supply a detector. LSDA addresses this mismatch by transferring knowledge about the difference between classification and detection.

The algorithm learns how the two tasks differ and applies that knowledge to category classifiers without bounding-box training annotations. It thereby converts those classifiers into detectors. The intended benefit is to extend detection to categories with abundant classification data but no corresponding box labels, reducing dependence on category-specific detection annotations.

Evaluation on the ImageNet LSVRC-2013 detection challenge supports the approach's effectiveness. Using classification data from ImageNet leaf categories, the authors produce a detector covering more than 7,600 categories. They also modify the architecture to run the 7,600-category detector at two frames per second. Detection for tens of thousands of categories is presented as a potential future reach of the method; the demonstrated scale is the reported 7,600-plus-category system.
neurips-2014-lsda-large-scale-detection-.tldr: LSDA transfers knowledge from classification to detection, enabling a demonstrated detector for more than 7,600 categories using available classification data.

paragraphs: A face image mixes information about identity with factors such as viewpoint and illumination. This makes learning identity features that remain useful across views challenging. The paper introduces the multi-view perceptron, or MVP, a deep model that separates identity and viewpoint representations while also generating views of the same face.

Given a single two-dimensional face image, MVP can infer a range of images showing different viewpoints. The motivation comes from the ability to recognize a person and imagine their appearance from another angle. The model brings recognition and multi-view image prediction into the same representation-learning approach, rather than treating identity features as its only output.

The authors report superior performance for MVP's identity features on the MultiPIE dataset. They also show that the model can interpolate and predict images at viewpoints absent from training. These are complementary findings: one concerns the usefulness of the learned identity representation, and the other concerns its ability to represent view changes. The reported results support the proposed separation of identity and view information in this setting.
neurips-2014-multi-view-perceptron-a-dee.tldr: MVP separates face identity and viewpoint features while predicting multiple views from one image, including viewpoints absent from training.

paragraphs: This paper develops a way to build prior distributions that respect structural constraints. Starting with a base distribution, it defines the prior through an information projection onto distributions supported by the desired constraint set. The construction connects an existing probabilistic model with knowledge about which variable configurations should be allowed.

When the exact projection is computationally intractable, the authors introduce parameterized approximations based on subsets of the domain. For sparse structure, they show that approximate inference using convex subsets is tractable and equivalent to a cardinality-constrained submodular maximization problem. Greedy forward selection consequently achieves at least a 1−1/e fraction of the optimal objective value for that problem.

The motivating application is prediction from high-dimensional functional neuroimaging data. The authors use a Gaussian base distribution induced by local partial correlations and construct priors encoding sparse support. Experiments on simulated and neuroimaging data show effectiveness in support recovery and prediction. The approximation guarantee concerns the specified optimization objective; it provides a principled computational route despite the general intractability of the optimal prior.
neurips-2014-on-prior-distributions-and-.tldr: Information-projected priors encode structural constraints, with a tractable sparse approximation that supports a 1−1/e greedy optimization guarantee.

paragraphs: Some classification measures, including the F-measure, cannot be expressed as sums of independent losses for individual examples. This complicates their theoretical analysis. The paper studies plug-in classifiers that estimate class probabilities and then apply a threshold selected from data, addressing a setting where the true probabilities are unavailable.

The authors provide a general consistency framework for measures that are continuous functions of true-positive and true-negative rates, provided their Bayes-optimal classifiers can be expressed by thresholding class probabilities. This condition matters: the framework relies on the optimal decision rule having a form the plug-in procedure can approximate. It moves beyond earlier results requiring exact knowledge of the underlying probabilities.

The framework yields consistency results for the F-measure and the geometric mean of true-positive rate and precision. For continuous distributions, the authors also establish consistency for any measure that is continuous and monotonically increasing in true-positive and true-negative rates. Experiments support the theory. These findings justify probability estimation followed by empirical threshold selection under the stated conditions, rather than guaranteeing consistency for every non-decomposable measure.
neurips-2014-on-the-statistical-consiste.tldr: The paper proves consistency of probability-estimation-and-thresholding classifiers for several non-decomposable measures under explicit conditions.

paragraphs: PEWA addresses image denoising by combining the outputs of several existing algorithms at the patch level. Its starting point is that different denoised versions of an image can supply material for a statistical aggregate. The paper proposes a general aggregation method, making the combination of those outputs the central contribution.

The authors show that even weakly denoised versions produced by standard methods can be used to compute an efficient patch-based estimator. The approach uses exponentially weighted aggregation and relies on MCMC sampling. This gives the combination a statistical foundation and provides a computational method for forming the resulting denoised estimate.

Experiments on real images compare PEWA with several competitive denoising methods. The authors report results comparable to the state of the art, rather than claiming that aggregation consistently exceeds every alternative. The finding is that a statistically grounded combination of patches from existing denoisers can itself be competitive. It also establishes that the intermediate denoised images need not already be strong final solutions to serve as useful inputs to the aggregation.
neurips-2014-pewa-patch-based-exponentia.tldr: PEWA statistically aggregates patches from existing denoisers using MCMC, achieving results reported as comparable to the state of the art.

paragraphs: Many high-dimensional estimators combine a smooth loss with multiple regularizers that express different structural preferences. This paper studies such superposition-structured, or dirty, models. It develops a family of second-order optimization methods for problems commonly approached with first-order techniques such as proximal gradient methods or ADMM.

The method forms a quadratic approximation to the smooth loss. Combined with the structured regularizer, this produces a subproblem that can be solved efficiently through alternating minimization. A general active-subspace selection procedure further accelerates the solver by using the low-dimensional structure encouraged by the regularizers. The authors also provide convergence guarantees.

Experiments on latent-variable graphical-model selection and multi-task learning report speedups exceeding tenfold over state-of-the-art first-order approaches when multiple regularizers are present. The authors describe their method as apparently the first to extend active-subspace ideas to multiple regularizers for these problems. The contribution links richer local approximations of the loss with structure-aware computation, and the reported speed gains concern the evaluated applications rather than all regularized estimation problems.
neurips-2014-quic-dirty-a-quadratic-appr.tldr: Quadratic loss approximations and active-subspace selection accelerate models with multiple regularizers, with reported speedups greater than tenfold.

paragraphs: A classifier may be trained on data drawn from a different distribution than the one it encounters in use. Reweighting training losses is a common response, supported by asymptotic arguments. This paper focuses on the finite-data difficulty: under substantial sample-selection bias, reweighting can produce large estimation errors.

The authors propose a minimax framework for learning a probabilistic classifier that adapts to different selection biases. Its information requirement is accurate estimates of statistics under the source distribution. Beyond that information, the formulation seeks as much robustness as possible to unknown aspects of the conditional label distribution, unless additional generalization assumptions are explicitly supplied.

This makes the treatment of uncertainty central to the learning problem. The framework distinguishes information supported by source statistics from assumptions about how labels generalize to the target distribution. Experiments on synthetic data and UCI binary classification tasks demonstrate its behavior and effectiveness. The stated robustness remains tied to accurate source-statistic estimates and to any explicit generalization assumptions incorporated into the formulation.
neurips-2014-robust-classification-under.tldr: A minimax classification framework handles sample-selection bias using accurate source statistics while remaining robust to unspecified label-distribution properties.

paragraphs: Analyzing calcium image sequences involves identifying cells and estimating their activity over time. This paper puts those tasks into one formulation. It seeks an extremely sparse representation of the sequence in terms of cell locations, cell shapes, spike timings, and impulse responses, combining spatial and temporal information within the same model.

A single optimization problem produces both cell segmentations and activity estimates. This is the central organizational choice: the quantities describing where cells are and how they behave are estimated within a unified problem. The method does not require heuristic preprocessing or postprocessing to obtain the reported outputs, making the optimization itself responsible for both parts of the analysis.

Experiments on real and synthetic data demonstrate that the approach is viable. The reported segmentation and activity estimates are on par with the state of the art, rather than claimed to be universally superior. The significance is that one sparse space-time formulation can achieve competitive results for both outputs together, providing an integrated alternative to handling cell identification and activity estimation as separate tasks.
neurips-2014-sparse-space-time-deconvolu.tldr: One sparse optimization problem jointly estimates cell segmentations and activity from calcium images, with competitive results and no heuristic pre- or postprocessing.

paragraphs: The power method computes dominant singular vectors through repeated matrix-vector operations. This paper analyzes its convergence when substantial noise is introduced after each multiplication. Treating these perturbed iterations as a general method allows a single analysis to cover applications that had previously required separate convergence arguments.

One application is streaming principal component analysis. The authors give a simpler, more general analysis that applies to arbitrary distributions, extending an earlier analysis based on a spiked covariance model. Even within that earlier model, they obtain quantitative improvements in a particular parameter regime. The broader framework also encompasses applications such as alternating minimization for matrix completion.

A second application is differentially private PCA. The proposed algorithm runs in nearly linear time in the input sparsity and achieves nearly tight worst-case error bounds. The authors further replace dimension dependence in the error with an essentially tight dependence on matrix coherence, yielding strong average-case improvements. The contribution is both a reusable noise-tolerant convergence analysis and sharper guarantees for specific spectral-learning tasks.
neurips-2014-the-noisy-power-method-a-me.tldr: A general convergence analysis of noisy power iterations strengthens guarantees for streaming PCA and efficient differentially private spectral analysis.

paragraphs: Sparse PCA presents a tension between statistical accuracy and computational tractability. Its global solution has an optimal statistical rate but is computationally intractable to obtain, while tractable convex relaxations can have weaker statistical rates. This paper combines a convex initialization with a nonconvex refinement to obtain an optimal principal-subspace estimator in polynomial time.

The refinement algorithm, sparse orthogonal iteration pursuit, has the desired guarantees only inside a restricted basin of attraction. The first stage therefore solves a convex formulation with early stopping to produce an initial estimate within that region. Initialization has a specific role: placing the estimate where the more accurate nonconvex procedure is theoretically reliable.

The analysis tracks computation and statistical error together. The initialization stage converges at a rate of 1/√t, while the main stage converges geometrically. The final estimator achieves a minimax-optimal statistical rate in sparsity, dimension, and sample size. The result supports a two-stage strategy whose success depends on reaching the required basin, rather than implying that arbitrary initializations make the nonconvex problem easy.
neurips-2014-tighten-after-relax-minimax.tldr: Convex initialization followed by nonconvex sparse orthogonal iteration achieves minimax-optimal sparse PCA estimation in polynomial time under the analyzed conditions.

paragraphs: Classifying high-dimensional signals on graphs is especially challenging when the underlying graph geometry is unknown. This paper introduces a Haar scattering transform that computes invariant signal descriptors in that setting. The approach combines a deep computational structure with a procedure for estimating the multiscale neighborhoods needed to organize the signals.

The transform uses repeated additions, subtractions, and absolute values to build a cascade of orthogonal Haar wavelet transforms. To estimate neighborhoods when the graph is unknown, the authors minimize an average total-variation objective. They use a pair-matching algorithm with polynomial complexity, providing a computational procedure for constructing structure at multiple scales.

The resulting representations are evaluated through supervised classification with dimension reduction. Tests use scrambled-image databases and signals sampled on unknown irregular grids on a sphere. These settings directly exercise the problem of unavailable geometry. The abstract reports the evaluation settings without claiming a particular performance advantage. The contribution is a representation-building method that couples inferred graph neighborhoods with a deep cascade of simple operations for subsequent classification.
neurips-2014-unsupervised-deep-haar-scat.tldr: Haar scattering builds invariant graph-signal descriptors through simple deep cascades while estimating unknown multiscale neighborhoods with polynomial-time pair matching.
